Explorative application of discrete Bayesian networks as surrogate models 
for energy systems analysis
Rainer Kelk
a , 1
, Luca Podofillini
a , *
, Vinh N. Dang
a
, Evangelos Panos
a , b
a
Centers for Nuclear Engineering and Science and for Energy and Environmental Sciences, Laboratory for Energy Systems Analysis,Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen PSI, 
Switzerland
b
Chair of Energy Systems Analysis, Institute of Energy and Process Engineering, ETH Zurich, Zurich 8092, Switzerland
HIGHLIGHTS
• We present methods for building, validating, and using BBNs as surrogate models.
• With average relative error below 2 %, the BBN model is an adequate model surrogate.
• Benefits: interactive analysis, intuitive uncertainty propagation, goal-driven analysis.
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Bayesian networks
Energy systems models
Surrogate models
Uncertainty propagation and analysis
ABSTRACT
This work investigates data-based discrete Bayesian Belief Networks (BBNs) as surrogate energy system models 
for result analysis and interactive analyses, such as what-if analyses. A simplified version of the Swiss TIMES 
(STEM) model, referred to as STEM-lite, is used for demonstration. A method to optimize the BBN model is 
devised, based on performance metrics related to the accuracy of the BBN predictions, calculated over data 
records unseen by the BBN in the training phase. Further validation of the BBN on a set of seven scenarios yielded 
an average relative error below 2 %, suggesting adequate performance as surrogate model. The application of the 
surrogate BBN model is demonstrated to highlight its benefits, which include enabling interactive analysis 
(supported by the visualization of key variables, their relationships and interactions), fast and intuitive uncer -
tainty propagation, and support for goal-driven analysis (backward reasoning from outcomes to the inputs that 
produce these outcomes). The surrogate BBN presented here was developed to elaborate the methods for con -
structing, validating, and using BBN models for energy systems analysis and to demonstrate the benefits of such a 
model; at this stage, this model is not intended for energy systems and economics policy discussions. For practical 
applications, future work is needed to reduce the number of data records to construct the BBN, to introduce the 
option to treat the time dependence of the input variables, and to allow for larger BBN models (involving more 
variables) that reflect the increasing complexity of energy systems.
1. Introduction
Energy systems models provide comprehensive and detailed repre -
sentation of the energy system sectors, from production to energy con -
version and consumption, and are typically used to identify energy 
system pathways that achieve one or more objectives under different 
policies, subject to technical, resource and other constraints [ 1 ]. Today, 
a primary application of energy system models is the achievement of 
sustainability in the context of climate change. The models are built with 
detailed technology specifications and often employ linear program -
ming techniques to minimize the overall cost of the energy provision. 
The generated outputs include estimates of technology capacity and 
utilization, marginal commodity prices, and emissions across the energy 
system. Some of the analytical strengths of energy systems models 
include a consistent framework for specifying techno-economic perfor -
mance, efficient goal-seeking within complex systems, and insights into

various energy futures aligned with policy objectives. The energy sys -
tems analysis space is typically multi-dimensional, spanning over energy 
technologies, commodities (e.g, electricity, gas, etc.), sectors (e.g., 
buildings, electricity sector, transport, etc.) as well as addressing mul -
tiple time and space scales. For this reason, the resulting mathematical 
model couples time, space and technology among the dimensions as well 
as within each dimension. The extensive scope of energy system models 
has led to increasing complexity as various approaches and features are 
developed to enhance the realism of internal model dynamics [ 2 , 3 ].
Due to the complexity of the problem and the large number of 
interdependent variables (e.g. policy parameters, technology costs, 
consumer needs and uses, sector coupling), the analyses can be 
computationally expensive (i.e. hours on standard computers). Also, 
interpreting the results in terms of the interactions among the variables 
and the model outputs requires expertise in energy economics and en -
ergy systems analysis, as well as familiarity with the underlying 
modelling frameworks. The treatment and communication of un -
certainties and the transparency of the connection among assumptions, 
models and the produced insights, e.g. in terms of the drivers of the 
results themselves and of the derived policy recommendations, are 
recurrently identified as areas in need of improvement [ 4 – 6 ].
When the computational demands of models are high, uncertainty 
propagation and analysis, sensitivity analyses, as well as prompt what-if 
analyses can be carried out by introducing surrogate models, compu -
tationally efficient approximations of more complex models. The use of 
simplified models to increase computational efficiency is established in 
energy systems analysis: heuristics and machine learning approaches are 
primarily used [ 7 – 10 ]. Dominant applications of machine learning 
address forecasting of prices and demands [ 7 , 8 , 11 ]. Applications of 
machine learning for energy system modelling has also received atten -
tion, as recent reviews point out [ 9 , 10 ], mostly to develop models from 
field data patterns, e.g. from smart meters and smart building sensors. 
Applications for surrogate modelling of energy systems models have 
used traditional approaches such as neural networks and support vector 
machines, with the primary objective of obtaining fast-running model 
approximations [ 12 , 13 ]. While offering an adequate solution to the 
computational speed, these machine learning approaches do not address 
the needs for transparent communication of results, of the associated 
uncertainty and policy recommendations.
The development of surrogate energy system models to support 
analysis and communication of the produced insights and the associated 
uncertainties is the subject of the present paper. The transparency of the 
surrogate model is emphasized in light of the growing demand for 
explainability in machine learning models, especially when these are 
used to inform policies with important societal implications [ 14 ]. In 
particular, this paper addresses graphical, probabilistic models for an 
intuitive visualization of the large-scale energy systems model variables 
and of their relationships: Bayesian Belief Network (BBN). The visuali -
zation capabilities of BBNs supports the explainability of the developed 
model [ 15 ]. The BBN network structure represents causality relation -
ships across variables, showing the chain of causal dependence from 
model inputs to results, therefore potentially allowing to explore the 
drivers of the results and of the recommended policies. BBN ’ s interactive 
framework lends itself to stakeholder involvement in the analysis of the 
results and implications. BBNs are typically used to represent and 
analyze uncertain knowledge through graph structures, i.e. Directed 
Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). The underlying relationships are estimated 
through statistical, probabilistic and computational methods, making 
Bayesian networks a combination of graph theory, probability theory, 
computer science, and statistics [ 16 ]. The BBN modelling flexibility is 
demonstrated by the large variety of application areas, e.g. natural and 
social sciences, engineering, finance, medical diagnosis [ 17 ]. For data- 
rich domains, BBN models can be constructed from the empirical data; 
in other cases, the BBN is constructed from expert judgment, e.g. for 
causal models of rare events. The foundation of BBNs in the Bayesian 
probabilistic framework also supports a formal combination of empirical 
and expert judgment data.
The research objective of the paper is to investigate and demonstrate 
the attractiveness of BBNs for surrogate modelling, in particular 
focusing on uses of interest for energy systems analysis, representation 
and propagation of uncertainty, goal-driven and what-if analyses. BBNs 
have been widely applied in the energy sector, as presented in recent 
review papers [ 18 – 20 ]. Data-driven BBN applications typically generate 
predictions concerning the energy market [ 21 – 24 ], electrical demand 
(e.g. from smart city data) [ 25 ], and renewable resource predictions (e. 
g. wind data series) [ 18 ]. Many studies exploit the BBN ’ s capability to 
support reasoning under uncertainty, generally for representation of 
causal relationships on uncertain variables. Examples include identifi -
cation and quantification of influences on prediction of carbon price 
[ 26 ], energy security [ 27 ], future demand for the water, energy, food 
nexus [ 28 – 30 ], reduction of CO
2 
emissions [ 31 – 33 ], effectiveness of 
policy and project implementation [ 34 – 36 , 37 ], optimal siting identifi -
cation [ 38 – 40 ]. Very recently, BBNs were used to investigate in -
terdependencies and related uncertainties among technologies within 
decarbonization pathways, as it emerges from ensembles of energy 
system model runs [ 41 ].
The energy model utilized in this work to explore the BBN applica -
tion is a simplified version of the Swiss TIMES energy model, developed 
in earlier work by [ 42 ], referred to as STEM-lite. The main simplifica -
tions introduced in STEM-lite relate to reducing: the scope of the Swiss 
TIMES model to the electricity sector only, the number of yearly time- 
slices (from 288 to 32), categorized into four seasons, with separate 
consideration for working days and weekends in each season; the 
number of periods in which the 2020 – 2050 time horizon is divided 
(three periods of 10 years each). Like STEM, STEM-lite is implemented 
in General Algebraic Modelling System (GAMS), an algebraic modelling 
language commonly used in energy system analysis [ 3 ].
The paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the 
basics of the BBN modelling tool, focusing on the BBN type adopted for 
the present demonstration: discrete BBNs. The section also presents the 
methodology to develop the BBN as a surrogate model, comprising three 
steps: STEM-lite data generation and discretization; identification of the 
optimal BBN with respect to specified performance metrics; validation of 
the optimal BBN on seven scenarios related to energy systems policy 
exploration. Section 3 demonstrates potential uses of the BBN as a sur -
rogate energy systems model, building on two scenario cases. Discussion 
and conclusions are given in Sections 4 and 5 , respectively.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Bayesian belief networks
In the qualitative BBN representation, the DAG, nodes denote 
random variables and edges indicate the presence of a relationship 
among these variables [ 16 , 17 ]. Basic concepts on BBNs are given in 
Appendix A. The direction of the edges indicates the direction of influ -
ence, with parent nodes influencing child nodes. The BBN node re -
lationships are quantified by conditional distributions. For discrete 
BBNs, i.e. BBNs where the nodes represent discrete random variables or 
a discretized representation of continuous variables, the relationships 
take the form of conditional probability distributions. For continuous 
BBNs, relationships are represented by conditional probability density 
functions. Hybrid BBNs combine discrete and continuous variables.
The present work adopts discrete BBNs: this is a common modelling 
strategy which, compared to continuous BBNs, allows using simpler 
learning and inference algorithms [ 43 – 45 ]. The GeNIe software package 
[ 46 ] was used for the BBN development and visualization.

Depending on the problem at hand and the data availability, 
different methods are used to build a BBN, blending expert knowledge 
and data in different ways and proportions, both to develop the BBN 
structure and to estimate the distribution parameters. The development 
of the BBN structure (i.e. the DAG) typically involves data-mining al -
gorithms to identify the causal relationships among the variables. These 
algorithms are data intensive, so that BBN structure learning is often 
aided by expert knowledge in the pre-selection of the most significant 
variables and links, and in the identification of the direction of influ -
ence. In many applications dealing with the causation of rare events, the 
DAG is fully derived by expert knowledge, exploiting a variety of 
knowledge elicitation techniques [ 17 ]. The quantitative relationships, 
the conditional distributions, can also be quantified solely using data, 
with distribution-fitting algorithms, combining data and judgment 
within a Bayesian framework, or directly via expert elicitation [ 47 ].
For the development of the surrogate model in the present paper, 
data-rich methods for BBN development are of interest. Indeed, STEM- 
lite ’ s computation time (about 3 s per run on a standard computer) al -
lows generation of many data records, up to 100,000 as presented in 
Section 2.3 . In particular, methods for BBN structure learning have been 
extensively studied in the literature and are typically distinguished as: 
score-based, constraint-based and hybrid [ 48 , 49 ]. Score-based methods 
evaluate different BBN models in the space and select the ones that 
optimize an information criterion, typically based on goodness-of-fit to 
the data. Constraint-based algorithms, on the other hand, perform a 
sequence of independence tests and construct a directed acyclic graph 
(DAG) based on the learned conditional independence relations. Hybrid 
algorithms combine elements from the two approaches.
For the present work, two structure learning algorithms were tested, 
both implemented in the GeNIe software package: Greedy Thick Thin -
ning (GTT) [ 50 ], and the Bayesian Search [ 51 ] algorithm, which are 
among the most used algorithms of the score-based type (note 
comparative study [ 48 ] shows that score-based algorithms are often 
faster and more accurate than constraint-based and hybrid). Preliminary 
tests resulted in the choice of the GTT algorithm, which consistently 
exhibited faster performances (up to more than two orders of magnitude 
in computing times) and comparable accuracy.
For the estimation of the BBN discrete conditional probability dis -
tributions, GeNIe implements the Expectation-Maximization (EM) al -
gorithm, which iteratively updates an initial distribution to maximize 
the likelihood of the available data [ 46 , 52 ].
2.2. BBN model development - overview
The process devised to develop the surrogate BBN model comprises 
three steps: 
1. Generation and discretization of the STEM-lite data for learning and 
validation
2. Optimization of the BBN structure and parameters
3. Scenario validation of the BBN as surrogate model
The first step ( Section 2.3 ) involves generation of STEM-lite input- 
output records and subsequent data discretization, for the records to be 
processed by the discrete BBN learning algorithm. Discretization of 
continuous variables must be done carefully, to avoid losing statistical 
accuracy and deriving inappropriate conclusions [ 44 ]. The approaches 
to variable discretization can be classified in: 1) manual, i.e. based on 
expert knowledge; 2) supervised, i.e. informed on the output variable, 
typically via optimization algorithms; 3) unsupervised, i.e. based on the 
distribution of the variable itself to be discretized [ 43 , 44 ]. The most 
widely applied approaches in BBN applications are manual and unsu -
pervised, the latter most frequently adopting equal-width or equal fre -
quency bins [ 43 , 44 ]. While supervised approaches are frequently 
adopted in the general computer science literature, their use for BBN 
modelling is still limited, due to both knowledge gaps and lack of 
implementation in most commercial software [ 44 ]. Manual discretiza -
tion, also known as expert discretization, involves the user manually 
selecting the thresholds for dividing the continuous data into discrete 
bins, on the basis of physical significance, theoretical knowledge, or the 
user ’ s expertise in the specific problem domain [ 44 ]. Anticipating the 
discussion in Section 2.3 , for the present application, the input variables 
( Table 1 ) were discretized with equal-width bins, while the other 
modelling variables were discretized manually, based on their distri -
bution from the input-output records.
The second step ( Section 2.4 ) determines optimal modelling choices 
affecting the BBN structure and the values of the BBN parameters (the 
Conditional Probability Distributions, CPDs): the number of discretiza -
tion bins for each node; the maximum allowed number of parents; the 
data set size (and its partition in training and validation data). As pre -
sented in Section 2.4 , the options for each of the three choices determine 
36 combinations (3 × 3 × 4, for the respective choice), therefore cor -
responding to 36 possible BBNs. Three evaluation metrics are used to 
determine the optimal BBN, two metrics relate to the BBN prediction 
accuracy, one relates to the BBN information content. Prediction accu -
racy is embedded into the GeNIe software and is calculated via confusion 
matrices based on 20 % of the input-output records, unseen by the BBN 
in the training phase.
For each node subject to the validation check, the BBN prediction is 
the node state with the largest probability, thus the prediction accuracy

metrics are based on single-state predictions. Therefore, accuracy-based 
validation does not address the whole BBN output of interest, i.e. the 
probability distributions associated to the output nodes. Also, any data 
record outside the most-likely discretization bin would be classified as 
wrongly predicted, thus penalizing predictions associated to wider dis -
tributions (see the discussion in Section 2.5 on this matter). To overcome 
these limitations of the accuracy-based validation, Section 2.5 presents 
the so-called “ scenario validation ” , where the node distributions of the 
optimal BBN are validated against STEM-lite runs on seven scenarios 
mimicking different policy investigation cases.
2.3. Data for BBN learning and validation (step 1)
Table 1 presents the STEM-lite inputs, used to generate the learning 
and validation data set, with the corresponding source. STEM-lite inputs 
include both fixed values, as well as uncertain variables ( Table 1 ). The 
values of the uncertain variables are sampled from Uniform distributions 
to generate the input-output records used to develop the surrogate BBN 
model. The uncertain variables include the costs of electricity produc -
tion technologies with the largest share in the Swiss energy mix, as well 
as gas and electricity import prices. The carbon tax value is explicitly 
considered as a representative policy instrument. Other policy in -
struments such as subsidies for renewable technologies can be implicitly 
incorporated within the costs of the associated technologies. The set of 
variables in Table 1 is chosen to investigate the BBN properties for 
simplified, yet representative case studies.
To further simplify model development for the present exploratory 
application, the STEM-lite uncertain input variables are modeled con -
stant over time, i.e. over 2030 – 2050. In practical terms, each sampled 
value for the uncertain variables is applied to all three time slices 2030, 
2040 and 2050 in input to STEM-lite. This simplification does not allow 
modelling price or subsidy trends over time, however some represen -
tation of input variability can be obtained via their marginal probability 
distributions defined for the base case scenario ( Section 3.1 ). Repre -
sentation of the time dynamics is an important subject of future work.
STEM-lite was run for each sampled combination of the uncertain 
inputs ( Table 1 ), obtaining 100,000 input-output records (to be divided 
into datasets of different sizes in the BBN learning phase). The input- 
output records are made of each sampled combination (inputs), and 
the STEM-lite generated values (outputs) for the 2030, 2040 and 2050 
amounts of electricity production from selected technologies (gas-fired 
and nuclear power plants, solar panels and wind turbines) and of the 
electricity import. As figures of merit for the energy configuration, the 
record includes the corresponding 2030, 2040, and 2050 CO2 emissions 
and marginal electricity costs (also referred to as outputs). Each data 
record includes values of 28 variables, i.e. 7 randomly generated input 
values and 21 STEM-lite generated values ( Fig. 1 ). Electricity production 
technologies such as hydropower and geothermal energy were not 
selected because of their small variability across the sampled records.
Discretization of the values in the input-output records was done 
differently for the input variables (uncertain variables in Table 1 and 
green boxes in Fig. 1 ) and the output variables (blue boxes in Fig. 1 ). The 
seven input variables were discretized with equal-width bins, a natural 
choice given their Uniform distribution, with number of bins to be 
determined based on the optimization procedure in Section 2.4 . The 
other variables (electricity production shares, CO2 emissions and mar -
ginal electricity costs in 2030, 2040, 2050) were manually discretized, 
based on their distribution from the 100,000 input-output records. 
Manual discretization was chosen because of the highly non-uniform 
and non-normal nature of the output distributions, see Fig. 2 for an 
example. The definitions and discretization intervals for all model var -
iables are given in Appendix B, obtained via visual inspection of each

distribution, as necessary making sure that the distributions peaks 
would be enclosed into one bin (as shown in Fig. 2 ). The GeNIe software 
convention is followed for the discretized state labels: labels in growing 
order, s1 representing the lowest absolute value. The label also includes 
the lower and upper thresholds of each state bin. Only integers are used, 
therefore for example in Fig. 2 , the second state “ s2 ” of “ Wind turbines 
production 2030 ” is named “ s2_0_0 ” .
Indeed, manual discretization can introduce biases in the BBN 
response, partly because the distribution informing the discretization (e. 
g. in Fig. 2 ) is conditional on the uniform distributions assumed for the 
input variables. Therefore, the same discretization intervals may not be 
optimal for other input distributions possibly assumed when the BBN is 
used for other applications. In addition, the definition (number and size) 
of the discretization intervals can be representative of the distribution of 
the specific variable to discretize, but not necessarily optimal for the 
overall BBN response. This is why the most advanced discretization 
approaches address variables jointly, not individually, as an optimiza -
tion problem, with objective function depending on the overall response 
[ 43 , 44 ]. As advocated in [ 43 , 44 ], the present paper adopts a compre -
hensive validation strategy both in the BBN optimization structure 
( Section 2.4 ) as well as for the final BBN structure selected for demon -
stration ( Section 2.5 ).
2.4. Optimization of the BBN structure and parameters (step 2)
The development of the BBN involves modelling choices affecting its 
structure and the values of the BBN parameters (its CPDs): the number of 
discretization bins for each input node (discretization for the other 
nodes is done manually); the maximum allowed number of parents; the 
data set size (with 80 % – 20 % split between learning and validation). In 
what follows, BBNs corresponding to each combination of choices are 
identified by the triplet ( “ # of bins ” , “ max parent ” , data set size). The 
evaluation metrics used to determine the optimal BBN are forward and 
backward accuracy and the parameter uniformity metric.
Concerning the accuracy metrics, in forward validation, the BBN is 
evaluated given evidence on the input nodes, in correspondence to the 
states associated to the discretized input values of the input-output re -
cord selected for validation (for the reader not familiar with BBNs, Fig. 5
can be referred to as an example of the developed discrete state BBN 
with green boxes as inputs and blue boxes as outputs, corresponding to 
the energy system model variable in Fig. 1 ). For each node of the BBN 
subject to validation, the node prediction (i.e. the node state with the 
largest probability) is compared to the corresponding discretized output 
state. A node-specific accuracy is calculated for all output nodes as the 
fraction of the correct predictions over the validation set: forward ac -
curacy is calculated as the average over all output nodes. In backward 
validation, evidence is assigned to the BBN output nodes, in corre -
spondence of the output values of the input-output record selected for 
validation. The most likely states of the input nodes are then compared 
to the discretized input values of the record. The backward accuracy 
metric is calculated based on the predictions concerning the input nodes 
(the most likely input values, not considering uncertainty) in the same 
way as the forward metric.
The BBN information content is accounted for by the parameter 
uniformity metric. The metric counts the number of CPDs that are still at 
their initial distribution (Uniform), i.e. no data was available for the 
corresponding parent state combination. The metric is the ratio of that 
number to the total number of CPDs. Low uniformity implies that a large 
fraction of the CPDs have been informed by data. The number of pa -
rameters of the BBNs subject to optimization varies from about 2500 for 
the smallest network, BBN (3,3,20k) to about 178,000 for the largest 
network, BBN (7, 7, 80 k), so it can very well be that the largest BBNs are 
overparametrized, i.e. including parameters that are not learned from 
data, nor subject to validation.
Fig. 3 shows the optimization metrics for the investigated combi -
nations: # of bins, max parents and data set size, respectively ordered in 
the figure. Note that the number of parameters required by the BBN 
options increases with all the BBN optimization variables (# of bins, max 
parents and data set size). In particular, for the latter, the larger the data 
set, the larger the number of links that are added because substantiated 
by data.
Forward accuracy increases in all three dimensions (blue circles in 
Fig. 3 ). Larger number of bins for input variables and of linked parents 
correspond to higher modelling flexibility and therefore higher accu -
racy. This is because the amount of generated data is sufficiently large 
that the validation data does not exercise the BBN outside the training 
range, for all BBN options. With respect to the sample size, forward 
accuracy tends to increase, albeit very slowly for some BBN options. This 
is because the increasing sample size provides more information to the 
BBN (hence the accuracy increase), but already at 20 k, the sample size is 
sufficient to cover satisfactorily the data records used for test. The 
increasing trend in forward accuracy with the sample size is more visible 
for larger BBNs (right part of Fig. 3 ), for which the larger sample sizes 
still provide useful additional information.
Backward accuracy (orange triangles) decreases with the number of 
discretization bins for the input variables (note the steps down at the 
continuous lines in Fig. 3 ). This is the result of the fact that in the data 
records originated by STEM-lite, multiple input variable combinations 
can lead to the same output variable combination. Therefore, when 
evidence is set for the BBN output nodes, the accuracy score is updated 
only if the corresponding input data combination matches the combi -
nation of the most likely states predicted by the BBN. In all other case, 
the mismatch is considered as wrong prediction. The larger the number 
of input bins, the larger the chances that the input combination from the 
data would not match the combination of the most likely input states as 
predicted by the BBN: hence the decreasing trend. Furthermore, still 
from Fig. 3 , backwards accuracy overall exhibits smaller values than 
forward accuracy: this is due to the larger uncertainty affecting the input 
nodes than output nodes, which again increases the chances of inaccu -
rate predictions. These aspects show a limitation of measuring accuracy 
based only on the most likely node state, not considering the node dis -
tribution. Indeed, the more comprehensive validation of Section 2.5 will 
be performed comparing the distribution predicted by the BBN to the 
one originated by the validation data.
Parameter uniformity (gray squares) is strongly affected by the 
maximum number of allowed parents, which in turn affects the number 
of BBN links (and therefore parameters). For BBN options with three 
parents maximum, the parameter uniformity is around 0.2, i.e. 80 % of 
the BBN relationships are informed by the data. For the other options, 
parameter uniformity is above or about 0.5, which entail over -
parametrized BBNs with large number of parameters not informed by 
data. Note also from Fig. 3 that uniformity is in practice independent on 
the sample size, except for the larger BBN options with seven dis -
cretization bins. This means that increasing the data does not inform

discretization bins, uniformity decreases for the BBNs with three parents

As a result of the above considerations, the BBN structure with five 
discretization bins for input variables and maximum three parents

adequate discrimination to support insights from the case studies in

3. Using the model: Scenario analysis results
The methods and results related to the development, optimization, 
and validation of the surrogate BBN have been presented in Section 2 . 
This section turns to the application of the BBN as a surrogate energy 
systems model, demonstrating three uses: 
• Representation of uncertainty in inputs and its propagation through 
the BBN model
• Goal-driven analyses, e.g. low CO2 emissions, with identification of 
input values to meet the goals ( “ Backward evidence propagation ” in 
BBN terminology)
• What-if analyses, exploring effect of changes in input values (of 
policy implementation) on the model outputs.
For all three uses, the speed and visualization capabilities of the 
surrogate model allows analysts to work interactively with the energy 
systems model.
Scenario analyses were carried out for eight cases, a base case sce -
nario and the seven scenario cases used in model validation ( Section 
2.5 ). In the base case, the BBN inputs are set to represent current values 
and their future trends are based on realistic assumptions. For the seven 
scenario analysis cases, the descriptor and the evidence setting are 
shown in Table 2 (second and third columns). An important difference 
between the BBN model runs carried out for model validation ( Section 
2.5 ) and those carried out for the scenario analyses discussed in this 
section concerns the initial input distributions. In model validation, 
uniforms distributions are used for these inputs ( Table 1 ); the aim is to 
validate the model over the entire analysis space. In contrast, for the 
application of the BBN, realistic distributions are used for these inputs – 
these correspond to the base case distributions. Nevertheless, given the 
simplifications introduced, namely the reduced set of modeled variables 
and their time invariance, the presented results are not intended for real- 
world policy decisions.

3.1. Base case scenario
The base case scenario involves assessing reference probability dis -
tributions for the six BBN inputs (green boxes in Fig. 5 ). The intuitive 
representation of the uncertainty in the inputs and of its propagation to 
the other model nodes is evident from Fig. 5 .
Concerning the assessment of the input distributions, the mode of the 
marginal distributions of technology investment costs, nuclear, wind, 
and solar, have been set based on current values: nuclear power in the 
8 – 11 kCHF/kW bin (state s2), wind turbines in the 1.9 – 2.6 kCHF/kW 
bin (state s3), solar PV in the 920 – 1280 CHF/kW bin (state s3). The 
distributions were defined considering that future cost reductions due to 
accumulated experience may be more likely than cost increases (this 
translates in larger probability masses for smaller values than for larger 
values than current). Possible subsidies for electricity production from 
wind and solar PVs also concur in decreasing future investment costs for 
these technologies.
The mode of the carbon tax is set on the 20 – 40 CHF/tCO2 bin, which 
correspond to CO2 prices before the 2022 energy crises [ 55 ]. The dis -
tribution represents that larger values are considered as more likely than 
smaller values, given current pricing trends and long-term decarbon -
ization goals.
Assessing electricity and gas import prices poses challenges due to 
uncertain developments and trends. The base case considers that the 
projected electricity import prices for the upcoming and the subsequent 
year are approximately 150 € /MWh [ 57 ] hence in the 137 – 191 CHF/ 
MWh bin. The intermittency of renewable sources, weather conditions, 
and emerging technologies introduce significant uncertainties to elec -
tricity prices, which are reflected in the relatively large tails of the 
marginal distribution for the electricity import price. Concerning gas 
import prices, the base case considers overall trends rather than extreme 
scenarios. Prior to 2021, gas prices in the Dutch TTF market remained 
below 30 € /MWh [ 58 ], hence in the 31 – 48 CHF/MWh bin. While 
geopolitical factors still contribute to some market uncertainty, current 
prices have returned to pre-2021 levels.
Analyzing the generation outputs in the base case, gas power plants 
still play a significant role in the generation capacity due to low gas 
import prices and the ongoing nuclear phase-out. Indeed, from Fig. 5 ,

4. Discussion and future work
The two scenario cases were designed to demonstrate the BBN 
application as surrogate energy systems models. As typical for surrogate 
models, once the model has been developed, BBN models are compu -
tationally fast, being based on simple mathematical relationships. An 
attractive feature for result presentation is the visualization of the node 
values directly on the model layout. Combined with the (in practice) 
real-time update of their values, node value visualization well supports 
user interaction on what-if analyses, exploration of policy options and 
energy system pathways, possibly during stakeholder demonstrations 
and decision-making discussion sessions. An example of this application 
is shown in scenario case 2 demonstrating the effect of low costs of 
electricity from renewable sources (e.g. obtained via subsidies) in the 
long-term electricity production mix.
Still related to visualization of the node values, BBNs offer an intu -
itive representation of the uncertainty in the inputs and of its propaga -
tion to the other model nodes, as shown in Fig. 5 , where the visualization 
of the input marginal distributions was used in support of the definition 
of the distributions by expert judgment. It is important to note that, 
while visual representation of the node distributions is attractive for 
communication and for model scrutiny, for large networks with many 
nodes it may become difficult for an analyst to understand the drivers for 
the node uncertainty. Indeed, while sensitivity analysis measures 
addressing the values and the probabilities of the BBN nodes are inte -
grated in the most common BBN software packages, the application of 
uncertainty analysis techniques (e.g. variance decomposition-based) is 
still at pioneering stage, see [ 61 ] for a recent application.
A distinguishing feature of BBNs is their support for backward 
inference (goal-driven inference), i.e. inferring the probability distri -
butions of the influencing factors, given evidence downwards on the 
causal chain. This was exploited in scenario case 1, where the distri -
butions of the input factors (representing simplifications of policy in -
struments) allowing for low long-term emissions was inferred. While the 
case study indeed includes several simplifications, a more comprehen -
sive and realistic BBN can be envisioned for exploration of policies and 
conditions resulting in the desired energy system performance metrics 
(e.g. low emissions, low dependence on import, low electricity pro -
duction costs).
The graphical representation with arrows connecting nodes allows 
visualizing the node influences as these emerge from the STEM-lite data 
records, allowing further understanding of the underlying energy sys -
tems model relationships. An example was presented in Section 3.2 , with 
reference to Fig. 6 . The BBN arrow connections (and lack of connections)

imply that low CO2 emissions in 2050 are driven by the value of the

interplay among gas power, wind turbine, and nuclear power electricity 
production discussed with reference to Fig. 8 and Fig. 9 .
Indeed, identification of the correct influences relates to the appli -
cability and performance of BBN structure learning algorithms, itself 
much influenced by the amount of data available. For the present work, 
the speed of the STEM-lite allowed the generation of large data sets; BBN 
models for realistic applications would need to be based on a smaller 
number of data records, potentially with a larger number of variables. 
This most likely would imply an increased use of expert judgment in the 
model structure development and resorting to different types of BBNs. 
Indeed, labelled node BBNs were a convenient choice for demonstration 
of the BBN framework features, and future work should envision the 
adoption of BBN models requiring fewer parameters (e.g. continuous or 
hybrid BBNs). In particular, continuous BBNs such as Additive Noise 
Models (ANMs) ([ 62 , 63 ]) and Additive Bayesian Networks (ABNs) [ 64 ] 
represent promising options for future investigation: besides lower data 
requirements compared to labelled node BBNs, these BBN types offer 
stronger guarantee for causal identifiability [ 58 ]. These advanced BBN 
implementations have been applied mostly in the context of epidemio -
logical and healthcare studies [ 64 ], therefore their adequacy for surro -
gate modelling will have to be assessed. Concerning the energy systems 
applications, future research would need to test BBN construction for 
realistic analysis cases, for example using scenarios generated from the 
models from [ 65 , 66 ]. Scaling up to realistic applications would involve 
not only computational aspects (such as dealing with larger networks 
and fewer data records), but also guidelines to select and define the BBN 
model nodes, depending on the foreseen application. Indeed, to deal 
with the computational challenges, one may not necessarily develop a 
full surrogate model of the energy system, but more specific (and 
therefore smaller) models each dedicated to address different decision- 
making issues.
The data sets generated for the purposes of the present paper, along 
with the more realistic data sets eventually generated from the models 
from [ 65 , 66 ] will constitute a platform for a systematic performance 
evaluation of different types of BBNs as well as more traditional surro -
gate modelling approaches based on machine learning techniques such 
as Artificial Neural Networks and random forests. It is worth also 
mentioning that, besides the advantages of continuous over discrete 
BBNs concerning causality representation and data requirements, the 
use of continuous BBNs resolves the challenges related to discretizing 
response [ 43 , 44 ], while however introducing significantly higher 
computational complexity. These data sets may be also used for a 
comparison of performance and trade-offs between different continuous 
and discretization BBN options.
Another important simplification to overcome relates to the treat -
ment of time. For the present application, model inputs were considered 
constant over the 2030 to 2050 time period, to decrease the size of the 
BBN model. The variables can still be interpreted as reference values for 
the whole period and allow deriving meaningful insights as demon -
strated in the preset paper, however a more informative BBN model 
should include time dependence on the inputs, e.g. recognizing that 
policies would not be implemented with constant effects over such a 
large time frame. Indeed, application of the dynamic BBN variant in 
energy systems modelling should be subject of future investigation.
5. Conclusion
This paper dealt with the use of BBNs as surrogate models for energy 
systems applications. A BBN was developed, based on data records 
generated by a simplified model, STEM-lite. The simplifications intro -
duced in the STEM model and in additional assumptions (e.g. on time 
dependence of input variables) were intended to reduce the computa -
tion time of single STEM runs and the number of model variables. This 
allowed working on a BBN based on discrete, labelled node, for which 
most of the available software packages (GeNIe software in the present 
work, [ 46 ]) offer implemented learning algorithms. Indeed, the aim of 
the work is to investigate and demonstrate the attractiveness of the 
modelling framework, eventually leaving the development of algo -
rithmic and computational advances for future work.
The working BBN used for demonstration was developed via an 
optimization process concerning the number of discretization bin for the 
input variables, the maximum allowed number of parent nodes, the data 
set size. For BBN validation, the present work developed BBN perfor -
mance measures beyond those typically considered in the literature, 
calculated over 20 % of the generated data records unseen by the BBN in 
the training phase. In particular, the parameter uniformity measure was 
developed to address how much the BBN is overparametrized with 
respect to the available data. Also, validation over the whole distribu -
tion of the target variables (referred to as “scenario validation”) was 
introduced as opposed to validation of only the reference BBN output (e. 
g. the most likely) for a comprehensive assessment of the BBN 
performance.
A scenario analysis was designed to demonstrate potential BBN ap -
plications, building on a base case and seven scenario cases. The base 
case and the scenario cases demonstrate three uses of BBNs for energy 
system modelling: representation of uncertainty in inputs and its prop -
agation through the BBN model, goal-driven analyses, with identifica -
tion of input values to meet the goals, what-if analyses, exploring effect 
of changes in input values (of policy implementation) on the model 
outputs. Indeed, these three uses are not mutually exclusive and can be 
combined as necessary. The main contribution of this paper is to un -
derscore the BBN attractiveness mainly concerning visualization of the 
original energy systems model relationships, fast and intuitive uncer -
tainty propagation, backward reasoning. These elements make BBNs a 
potentially useful tool for energy policy investigation and demonstra -
tion, eventually in panel and workshop sessions with experts and diverse 
stakeholders.
Other potentially attractive features, not exercised in the present 
work, include BBN’s modularity and suitability to represent uncertain 
effects. Modularity entails the possibility of combining multiple BBNs, 
each developed from different energy systems models, thus building a 
progressively more comprehensive surrogate increasing its modelling 
scope, e.g. adding the transportation sector to the model. Also, the 
probabilistic nature of BBNs makes these particularly suitable to 
modelling of “soft influences”, e.g. those related human factors. For 
energy systems applications, this could be useful to represent uncer -
tainty in the adoption of policies, consumer behaviors and socio- 
economical influences.
Building on the attractive features, exploiting BBNs for practical 
purposes in energy systems modelling requires overcoming a number of 
simplifying assumptions made in the present work. In particular, this 
would involve dealing with smaller sets of data records to train the BBN, 
allow for time dependence in the input variables, and generally dealing 
with larger BBN models (i.e. involving more variables). The identified 
directions of future research work involve adoption of BBN variants with 
smaller number of parameters (e.g. continuous or hybrid), incorporating 
dynamics, more extensive use of expert judgment to develop the BBN 
structure.
